analysis.one_liner: Adds hearing aids and hearing rehabilitation services to Medicare coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on Nov. 20, 2025, and referred to two House committees with no further action so far.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare does not pay for hearing aids or services to fit and adjust them, so millions of older Americans pay thousands of dollars out of pocket. The HEAR Act would change Medicare to cover hearing aids plus hearing assessments, fittings, adjustments, and rehabilitation by licensed professionals. It would apply starting between one and three years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss, especially older adults on fixed incomes who currently pay out of pocket for hearing aids, which commonly cost thousands of dollars per device.

how_it_helps.text: Adds hearing aids to Medicare's list of covered durable medical equipment and adds aural rehabilitation services to the covered outpatient benefit [S3].

Coverage includes a comprehensive audiologic assessment, hearing aid evaluation, fitting and adjustment, instruction on use, periodic refittings, and counseling such as speech reading and auditory training [S3].
Removes hearing aids and examinations for them from Medicare's list of explicitly excluded items, reversing a decades-old coverage gap [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program and its taxpayers and premium payers bear the new cost; the bill includes no dedicated funding or offset for it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare program, taxpayers, and premium payers

drawbacks.text: The bill adds an open-ended federal benefit with no dedicated financing or spending offset, which would increase Medicare outlays and pressure on premiums and general revenue [S3].

It excludes over-the-counter hearing aids from coverage, so the cheaper devices approved for sale without a prescription would not be covered — Medicare would pay only for professionally fitted prescription devices [S3].

Replacement is limited: a person must go at least three years without a new hearing aid, and must show their hearing has deteriorated so that a different type is appropriate, which could leave some users waiting [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 30 million-plus Americans with hearing loss, including most Medicare beneficiaries, the benefit is direct and substantial: hearing aids today are almost entirely out-of-pocket. The cost is real but typical of Medicare benefit expansions, and the bill is unusual among such bills in that it specifies covered services and replacement limits rather than leaving everything to regulators. Its main design weakness is the lack of a funding source.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House on Nov. 20, 2025, and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it awaits any action.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Mullin (D-CA) introduced the HEAR Act of 2025 on Nov. 20, 2025, with six cosponsors — five Democrats and one Republican [S1] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled [S5].
Because provisions touch two committees' jurisdictions, the Speaker referred it to both, meaning it must win attention in two committees to advance [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has been affected yet — the bill has only been introduced and referred to committees, so nothing has been gained or lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; awaiting committee action

for.name: Rep. Kevin Mullin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add hearing aids and hearing rehabilitation to Medicare coverage.

for.name: Rep. Mike Lawler
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a bipartisan sponsor team — one Republican among the seven original backers — but no opposition has been recorded because no vote or hearing has taken place.

industries.note: Medicare coverage would create a large new pool of paying customers for professionally fitted hearing aids. The bill excludes over-the-counter devices from coverage, which also protects the higher-priced fitted-device market.

Coverage of assessments, fittings, refittings, and rehabilitation would make audiologists the providers of a new Medicare benefit. Seniors gain access at the same time providers gain a reimbursement stream, so their interests run together here.

analysis.trajectory: A brand-new bill with six cosponsors sitting in two committees faces long odds: most Medicare benefit-expansion bills never get a hearing or markup, and because this one would add spending without an offset it would also need a way past fiscal rules if it ever reached the floor. Barring a push from leadership or inclusion in a larger health package, it is likely to sit without action for the rest of this Congress.
